subtype: Approach: setting a mini goal to show family [Action]
passage: Monday. Asif's magic book was full of tricks, but he had finished none of them. "Diwali is in three weeks," he told his cousin Deepika on the phone. "I will do three tricks for everyone." Now he had a deadline. The next Saturday Asif practised the coin trick twenty times in front of the mirror, dropped the coin nine times, and started a tick chart. Diwali night. In the living room, in front of all the cousins, his hand shook a little, but the coin vanished on the first try. Deepika clapped her hands and screamed, "Do it again!" By the third trick his grin was wider than anyone's.

qa.q: How many tricks did Asif plan to perform?
qa.a: Asif planned to perform three tricks.

qa.q: How did Asif feel in front of his cousins, and what showed it?
qa.a: Nervous but excited, since his hand shook a little yet he was grinning by the third trick.

qa.q: What could Asif do if a trick fails on Diwali night?
qa.a: Laugh, make it part of the show and move on to the next trick, because his practice has prepared him.

qa.q: How might Deepika see the show?
qa.a: Delighted and impressed, since she screamed and asked for the coin trick again.

grounding: A boy learning magic sets a mini goal to perform three tricks for cousins on Diwali, and the deadline shapes his practice.

subtype: Approach: setting a mini goal to show family [Action]
passage: Nilesh, you think your Raghav Dada only knows how to read the newspaper? When I was ten, a travelling magician came to our school and I wanted to be him. I got a thin book of tricks at the fair. For a month I fiddled with it and learnt nothing properly. Then Amma said all the cousins were coming for Diwali, seven weeks away. I said, "I'll do a show." Three tricks, no more: the vanishing coin, the rope that joins itself, the card that jumps to the top. I gave each trick two weeks, practising every evening in front of the steel almirah mirror, and kept the last week for all three together. On Diwali night I dropped the coin once. The cousins clapped anyway, loudest for the rope.

qa.q: How many weeks away was Diwali when Raghav planned the show?
How might young Raghav have felt during the month before the Diwali plan?
qa.a: He probably felt stuck and a bit frustrated, fiddling with the book of tricks without learning anything properly.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story gave Raghav's practice its shape?
qa.a: Promising a three-trick show for the cousins at Diwali: the fixed date let him give each trick two weeks and keep the last week for a full run-through.

qa.q: What might the Diwali show have been like for the cousins?
qa.a: They seem to have enjoyed it, clapping even after the dropped coin, which suggests they cared more about the fun than about a perfect show.

grounding: An elder recalls how a Diwali show for cousins gave a clear shape to weeks of magic-trick practice.

subtype: Approach: setting a mini goal to show family [Action]
passage: Tenzin had three weeks until Diwali, when all eleven cousins would squeeze into Masi's flat. He wanted to do a show: three tricks, polished. The trouble was time. Tuition took two evenings a week, and his little sister Madhuri kept borrowing the rope for her doll's swing. So he wrote the plan on the back of his maths notebook: week one, coin vanish; week two, card rise; week three, rope trick, then all three together on the last two days. He practised twenty minutes on non-tuition nights and hid the rope in his school bag. In week two he still fumbled the card, so he dropped a fancy flourish and kept the trick simple. On Diwali night Madhuri held the hat, and nobody noticed the card came up a bit crooked.

qa.q: How many cousins were coming for Diwali?
qa.a: All eleven cousins were coming, to Masi's flat.

qa.q: What might Tenzin have been worried about when he wrote the plan?
qa.a: He was probably anxious about having only three weeks, with two tuition evenings a week and the rope going missing, and feared the tricks wouldn't be ready.

qa.q: What else could Tenzin do if a trick still wasn't ready near Diwali?
qa.a: Cut it down, as he did with the card, or do only two tricks well, because a small polished show beats three shaky ones.

qa.q: What might the show be like for Madhuri?
qa.a: Holding the hat lets her be part of it, so she may feel proud and included rather than just the one who kept taking the rope.

grounding: Shows a boy using a Diwali show for his cousins as a deadline to plan weekly magic practice despite little time.
